newsitem.title: POLAND: Stolpe in Poland to discuss flood measures.
newsitem.headline: Stolpe in Poland to discuss flood measures.

text.p: German and Polish officials met on Thursday to discuss ways of regulating the Oder River which runs along the border and has flooded large areas of both countries.

Polish Finance Minister Marek Belka said after meeting Manfred Stolpe, the premier of the neighbouring German state of Brandenburg, that the project might be jointly financed by Poland, Germany and the European Union.
"We will discuss the topic further and are awaiting comments from the German side," PAP news agency quoted Belka as saying.
Stolpe, visiting Poland for two days, was later due to meet Interior Minister Leszek Miller to discuss improving coordination of flood relief efforts.

The Polish town of Slubice on the Oder was maintaining a virtual ban on car traffic for the third day in a row because of fears that vibrations could cause its sodden dikes to burst and submerge it under five meters of water.

"Soldiers and volunteers, who continue to heroically fight to keep the dike from cracking, have to carry sandbags about 100 metres (yards) on their backs because delivery vehicles can't approach any closer," said Marek Sobczak of the government's crisis committee.

The Oder had subsided about two cm (one inch) in 24 hours in Slubice, but remained dangerously high at 2.5 metres above alarm levels, just as it did in many other towns througout flood-hit southern and western Poland, Sobczak said.

On the German side, where the flooding has been less severe than in Poland, thousands of soldiers were laying down five-tonne sandbags to prevent a damaged dike near Hohenwutzen bursting open and unleashing a catastrophic flood over 250 sq km.

The Polish weather institute said it expected light rain in the affected areas of the country area on Thursday with heavier rain in central regions on Friday, but that this was not likely to cause new flooding.
Saturday was likely to bring more light showers in the south, with a possibility of thunderstorms.

Fifty-four people have died in what has become Poland's worst flooding disaster, and 162,000 people have been evacuated over the last three weeks. Of these, nearly 50,000 were still homeless, Sobczak said.

He said that in the previous 24 hours, floods had covered another 840 hectares (2,070 acres) of land but receded from more than 6,500 hectares. Flood waters presently cover nearly 1,900 square km (730 sq miles) of Poland.
The government has begun the massive task of reconstruction in the affected areas and the finance ministry wants to introduce a special flood tax next year to help finance the rebuilding.

Opposition parties have strongly criticised the ruling coalition of ex-communists and peasants for the way they have handled the flood crisis. The latest opinion polls show the coalition losing popularity as a result of the disaster with less than two months to go to parliamentary elections.
